assessment: The discussion cites a separate cinnamon and clove essential oil nanogel study of rodent nociception. Neither spice was tested in the dill trial.
Cinnamon and clove occur in cited topical studies. The dill trial measured itch, skin dryness, sleep and itch-related quality of life without a spice arm or anxiety endpoint.
Capsaicin is discussed in prior topical itch studies, including application-site burning. It was absent from the dill trial arms.
The cited nigella trial measured oxidative stress, inflammation and glycemic outcomes. Nigella was absent from the dill trial arms.

Topical sesame oil served as the vehicle and as a comparator. The trial measured itch, skin dryness, sleep and itch-related quality of life in dialysis patients without a separate pain, anxiety or depression endpoint.
Sweet almond oil appears in cited topical uremic itch work. No almond oil arm or depression outcome appears in the dill trial.
The experiment fed perilla seed oil to mice, with a soybean oil control diet and a fish oil comparator. The methods list no sage exposure.
Alpha-linolenic acid describes the perilla seed oil. The mice did not receive flaxseed oil, and this diet study does not establish a clinical effect of flaxseed oil.
The paper evaluated odor pleasantness and familiarity in healthy women. Fatigue appears as a possible order effect of testing, with no measured fatigue outcome.

Ginger appeared in a mixed meal preceding exercise-associated dysphagia and stomach cramping. The patient later ate the ingredients separately without systemic symptoms. The case does not isolate ginger or measure Parkinson pain.
The trial calls perilla Japanese basil. The intervention used Perilla frutescens leaf extract and did not test culinary basil.
Rosmarinic acid was a constituent of the perilla leaf extract. The trial measured gastrointestinal discomfort and bowel function without a sage arm.

The placebo trial found nearly identical increases in days with stools and no clear constipation-score difference. Participants were otherwise healthy adults and received extract made from dried leaves.

Tarragon extract in feed improved social interaction and grooming after social defeat. The sucrose preference comparison was inconclusive. The animal measures leave clinical depression after dried culinary tarragon open.
Rosmarinic acid characterized the summer savory extract. The study tested cisplatin-related anxiety-like behavior with no sage arm.
Oral summer savory extract was tested in cisplatin-treated rats. The outcomes included maze behavior and biochemical measures, without a nociception or pain scale.
Ginger occurs in a reference title. The intervention was summer savory extract without a ginger arm.
Cranberry juice appears in cited oxidized-LDL research. This trial tested perilla leaf powder and did not include a cranberry arm or report depression.
Oral oregano extract attenuated anxiety-like maze and open-field changes in chronically stressed rats. The experiment did not test dried culinary oregano or clinical anxiety.

assessment: Sodium benzoate was a standard fly feed preservative. The experiments tested curry leaf, nettle and chamomile extracts with rotenone and did not measure cinnamon-related fatigue.
An oregano leaf hexane extract attenuated anxiety-like behavior in rats with experimental hepatic encephalopathy. The preparation and model differ from the frozen comparison.
Topical cinnamon essential-oil gel reduced late-phase rat formalin pain scores without a clear hot-plate effect. Ground spice and Parkinson pain were untested.
